facts.userPrompt: Quiero hacer un recorrido a pie por el centro de la Ciudad de Mendoza, sus plazas y lugares históricos.
facts.systemPrompt:
Interpret the user's supplemental tourism preferences into normalized intent.
Return JSON only. You interpret language; deterministic code enforces the result.
Never invent geographic entities, provider IDs, coordinates, or evidence.
Do not turn ambiguity into a hard rule. Preserve uncertainty in ambiguities.
For positive preferences, output preferredFacets as a list of objects with:
- dimension: active dimension name (theme, trait, intent, winery_scale, tourism_intensity, nature_type, local_character). Do NOT output exploration_style.
- key: CANONICAL domain key in English (e.g. "architecture" not "arquitectura", "food" not "comida", "walk" not "caminata", "history" not "historia").
- Map history to theme and walk to intent. nature_type is only for mountain, forest, coast, river, desert, or park. local_character is only for authentic, residential, traditional, or contemporary. A named neighborhood such as San Telmo is an anchor, not local_character.
- confidence: float between 0 and 1 indicating certainty.
- strength: "strong" | "medium" | "weak" indicating user emphasis.
- evidence: one or more short excerpts copied from the user's text that support
  this facet. Never invent evidence; facets without supporting excerpts are rejected.
Do not invent arbitrary importance numbers; code derives importance deterministically from strength.
Also output anchoredPlaces: concrete named places/areas/routes the user explicitly mentioned by
name (never a generic theme). For each, output:
- rawName: the name as mentioned by the user.
- usage: "geographic_scope" | "specific_destination" | "named_path" | "unknown". This describes how the phrase uses the name, not what geographic entity it is.
- priority: "must" ONLY for explicit, unambiguous named-place intent, for example
  "quiero visitar X", "incluí X", "sí o sí quiero ir a X", "no me quiero perder X".
  Anything weaker or ambiguous -- including a place mentioned only in passing while
  describing a theme, e.g. "me interesa la arquitectura de X" -- is priority "soft".
Extract anchors conservatively: when in doubt about the name or the intent, omit the anchor
rather than guessing. Do not invent named places that were not mentioned.
Other fields: excludedThemes, excludedTraits, hardExclusions, softConstraints, ambiguities,
dietaryPreferences, accessibilityPreferences, budgetPreferences, groupPreferences,
positiveSemanticQuery, notes. Use short lowercase phrases.

facts.content:
### 1. City of Mendoza

Gobierno Ciudad de Mendoza

Discover the City of Mendoza in a day filled with flavors, history, and nature! Start your day with breakfast at places like [Brod](https://www.instagram.com/brodbakery/) or [Monono](https://www.instagram.com/monono.ar/), or at one of the cafes on Colón Street, perfect for fueling up for a day of walking. Sarmiento Pedestrian Street, inaugurated in 1989 and home to historic buildings like the San Martín Passage, famous for its French stained glass windows, is a popular spot for shops, workers, and locals.

Continue your journey through Plaza Independencia, the city’s main square, and the perfect place to relax and watch the daily flow of people. From there, head to Central Park, a modern green space with playgrounds, an artificial lake, and a collective mural showcasing local artists' creativity.

For lunch, there are various options to suit all tastes on streets like Juan B. Justo, Arístides, or the [Central Market](https://www.instagram.com/mercadocentralmza/), which host numerous spots to recharge. In the afternoon, explore the Paseo Alameda, a historic path lined with rose gardens and the San Martín House, where you can learn more about Argentina’s liberator.

[…]

### 2. General San Martín Park

Gobierno de Mendoza

General San Martín Park is the green lung of Mendoza. Designed by French landscaper Carlos Thays, it is considered the largest artificial park in South America. It's the perfect place for sports activities and leisurely walks.

Within the park, you’ll find numerous cultural and artistic points of interest. The entrance gates are iconic, along with the Fountain of the Continents and the lake. Also noteworthy is the [Cornelio Moyano Museum](https://www.instagram.com/museomoyano/), an example of modern architecture in the rationalist style and a great spot for kids to learn more about local fauna and flora. The park also offers various dining options, such as cafes, craft breweries, juice bars, and ice cream trucks. Exploring the park can take several hours, so comfortable shoes and a map or GPS app are recommended.

Tip: You can find free walking tours throughout the year on the [City of Mendoza's website](https://ciudaddemendoza.gob.ar/2023/12/27/free-walking-tour-para-arrancar-el-2024-y-conocer-la-ciudad/).

Advertising

### 3. Cerro de la Gloria

Ciudad de Mendoza/Ph: Estefanía Tapia

Cerro de la Gloria is located within General San Martín Park. Its name was officially changed in 1913 to honor the Army of the Andes.

Reaching the summit is easy, with pedestrian paths (get ready to walk!) and paved roads for vehicles, with several viewpoints along the way. Parking is available for cars and buses, along with restrooms and a police station in the area.

At the top stands the Army of the Andes Monument, inaugurated in 1914 to commemorate General José de San Martín's crossing of the Andes. This work by sculptor Juan Manuel Ferrari features an equestrian statue of San Martín, surrounded by figures representing key moments of the independence campaign. The monument, standing 16 meters high, symbolizes the fight for freedom and is adorned with the crests of Argentina, Chile, and Peru.

Tip: There's a [small food stall](https://www.instagram.com/cerrodelagloria.arboleda/) where you can enjoy a coffee and take panoramic photos of the surrounding mountains.

### 4. Chacras de Coria

Cámara de Turismo de Mendoza

Chacras de Coria is a charming town located in the Luján de Cuyo department, named after the Coria family who arrived many years ago. Plaza Gerónimo Espejo, founded in 1902, is the heart of the town and honors a leader of the independence campaign alongside General San Martín.

The Church of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, inaugurated in 1935, is the town’s religious center, notable for its colonial style, and located around Espejo Square. The Paso de los Andes Station, opened in 1890 and closed in 1984, once connected Mendoza with Los Andes in Chile. Although a fire in 1950 destroyed much of its structure, its English-style architecture still stands and is being restored to become a cultural space.

Chacras de Coria’s historic center is filled with old mansions and murals by local artists. The Luján de Cuyo region is also home to many wineries, some offering boutique accommodation. Notable wineries include [Clos de Chacras](https://www.instagram.com/closdechacras/), [Cruzat](https://www.instagram.com/bodegacruzat/), [Altavista](https://www.instagram.com/bodegaaltavista/), and [Nieto Senetiner](https://www.instagram.com/nietosenetiner/).

**You might also like:** [8 Boutique hotels to relax in Chacras de Coria](https://www.timeout.com/buenos-aires/mendoza/boutique-hotels-chacras-de-coria-casa-glebinias-susana-balbo)

[…]

### 5. Cacheuta Hot Springs

Gobierno de Mendoza

Cacheuta Hot Springs is an ideal destination for relaxation, located just 39 km from the City of Mendoza. Open year-round, the [thermal water park](https://www.instagram.com/parque_de_agua_termascacheuta/) offers access to over 10 pools filled with 100% thermal water. Highlights include stone pools, a 270-meter lazy river, and a wave pool with a 10-meter-high spray. The park also offers picnic areas with barbecue facilities.

For those seeking wellness, the [Hotel & Spa Termas Cacheuta](https://www.instagram.com/hotel_spa_termascacheuta/)—also open year-round—offers hydrotherapy and treatments like mud therapy and dry saunas, available for guests 14 years and older. Visitors can opt for the Full Day TermaSpa experience, which includes a buffet lunch with traditional Argentine dishes. There is also an afternoon spa option, available from 3 to 6 p.m., for a relaxing getaway.

Tip: Mendoza can be hot towards the end of spring and throughout summer, so we recommend visiting the hot springs on cooler days. There’s a small village nearby with restaurants, shops, and cafes, perfect for a day trip to enjoy with a full belly, a happy heart, and a calm body.
